Abstract: Imagine a near future where advanced humanoid robots, powered by multimodal large language models (MLLMs), effortlessly interpret real-time sensing data, not just from their own sensors, but also from neighboring drones, autonomous vehicles, or underwater vehicles. Such robots for the physical AI are already taking shape in laboratories, hinting at imminent deployment across industries to tackle tasks like warehouse logistics, manufacturing, factory assembly, precision agriculture, public-space assistance, and on-site medical or safety rescue. While a single robot can demonstrate impressive local autonomy, realistic missions demand holistic coordination among multiple agents, compelling them to share and jointly interpret vast streams of sensor information. In these high-stakes scenarios, communication is indispensable, since without robust links, each robot remains blind to the broader mission context and cannot leverage the combined intelligence offered by a collective MLLM. Yet transmitting comprehensive sensor data from dozens or hundreds of robots, each with its own bandwidth and latency constraints, can overwhelm networks. This challenge is exacerbated when a system-level orchestrator or cloud-based MLLM needs to fuse multimodal inputs to generate holistic decisions, like route planning, anomaly detection, or real-time adjustments to complex collaborative tasks. Crucially, these tasks are often initiated by high-level natural language instructions (e.g., “Search for the yellow bin”). This text-based intent serves as a powerful filter for resource optimization: by understanding the specific goal via MLLMs, the system can selectively activate only the relevant sensing modalities, dynamically allocate communication bandwidth, and determine the optimal computation placement. This “intent-to-resource” mapping capability is a fundamental motivation for the proposed unified architecture. Moreover, many real deployments require open-vocabulary perception and language-grounded action (e.g., recognizing previously unseen objects or infrastructure outside the robot’s field-of-view), which is difficult to achieve with closed-set on-device perception alone. Viewed this way, R2X is fundamentally an intent-to-resource orchestration problem: given a high-level language command and system context, the network must jointly optimize sensing, wireless communication, and computation so that task-level success is maximized under resource constraints. This survey examines how integrated sensing, communication, and computation design paves the way for effective multi-robot coordination under MLLM guidance. We begin by reviewing state-of-the-art sensing modalities (from bounding-box LiDAR to hyperspectral imaging) and their interplay with semantic or partial-compression techniques. Next, we analyze communication strategies, including low latency protocols, edge-based orchestration, and adaptive resource allocation, to ensure scalable and timely data delivery at scale. We then explore distributed, hybrid, and fully centralized computing approaches, highlighting how large-model reasoning can be split among on-device distillation and powerful edge/cloud servers. To ground these concepts in measurable outcomes, we further present four end-to-end demonstrations that make the orchestration loop explicit (sense  $\rightarrow $  communicate  $\rightarrow $  compute  $\rightarrow $  act): 1) digital-twin warehouse navigation with semantic sensing and predictive link context; 2) mobility-driven proactive MCS control under delayed feedback; 3) a real FollowMe robot with a practical semantic-sensing switch over WiFi; and 4) real-hardware open-vocabulary trash sorting where an edge-assisted MLLM grounds text instructions to unseen objects and out-of-FOV bins via multi-view sensing. Ultimately, our goal is to guide the robotics research community and industry practitioners in devising end-to-end solutions that integrate sensing, communication, and computation for real-time and large-scale multi-robot operations. By uniting advanced sensors, flexible network design, and MLLM-based intelligence, autonomous robot teams can achieve a truly holistic awareness and responsiveness in the complex environments of tomorrow. Across the demonstrations, we emphasize system-level metrics—payload size, end-to-end latency, reliability, and task success—to clarify when and why R2X-style edge/communication-assisted orchestration provides tangible advantages over purely on-device baselines.

Abstract: Deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) in embodied AI applications manifests a significant bottleneck between high-performance reasoning and hardware-constrained edge deployment. While cloud-based inference is hindered by network latency and instability, edge-deployed monolithic small-scale models often suffer from reasoning degradation and instruction hallucinations. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a low-latency and low-hallucination edge compound AI system integrated with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). By implementing task decoupling, a lightweight LLM manages high-level logical reasoning and routing, while a compact Vision-Language Model (VLM) handles real-time visual perception. This work provides an efficient and robust solution for autonomous robotics in edge environments.

Abstract: In the fifth-generation (5G) era, eliminating communication interference sources is crucial for maintaining network performance. Interference often originates from unauthorized or malfunctioning antennas, and radio monitoring agencies must address numerous sources of such antennas annually. Autonomous aerial vehicles (AAVs) can improve inspection efficiency. However, the data transmission delay in the existing cloud-only (CO) artificial intelligence (AI) mode fails to meet the low latency requirements for real-time performance. Therefore, we propose a computer vision-based AI of Things (AIoT) system to detect antenna interference sources for AAVs. The system adopts an optimized edge-cloud collaboration (ECC+) mode, combining a keyframe selection algorithm (KSA), focusing on reducing end-to-end latency (E2EL) and ensuring reliable data transmission, which aligns with the core principles of ultrareliable low-latency communication (URLLC). At the core of our approach is an end-to-end antenna localization scheme based on the tracking-by-detection (TBD) paradigm, including a detector (EdgeAnt) and a tracker (AntSort). EdgeAnt achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance with a mean average precision (mAP) of 42.1% on our custom antenna interference source dataset, requiring only three million parameters and 14.7 GFLOPs. On the COCO dataset, EdgeAnt achieves 38.9% mAP with 5.4 GFLOPs. We deployed EdgeAnt on Jetson Xavier NX (TRT) and Raspberry Pi 4B (NCNN), achieving real-time inference speeds of 21.1 (1088) and 4.8 (640) frames/s (FPS), respectively. Compared with CO mode, the ECC+ mode reduces E2EL by 88.9%, increases accuracy by 28.2%. Additionally, the system offers excellent scalability for coordinated multiple AAVs inspections. The detector code is publicly available at https://github.com/SCNU-RISLAB/EdgeAnt.

Abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) are increasingly used for real-time image processing, augmented reality, mobile robotics, and autonomous driving. This paper introduces a new Deep Neural Network Partitioning Strategy (DNNPaS) for Optimizing End-to-End Latency in Dynamic Mobile Edge Computing. DNNPaS uses an external machine learning model to predict the latency of each DNN layer and data transmission. This external machine learning model gets the client and edge device metrics along with network conditions to predict the optimal partition point of the DNN model. Our method dynamically adjusts to diverse network environments and server conditions, offering a robust solution for deploying DNNs on resource-constrained devices with improved overall performance.

Abstract: Autonomous Internet-of-Things (IoT) devices deployed at the extreme edge—such as nano-drones, industrial actuators, and nanosatellites—must make safety-critical decisions within sub-millisecond deadlines while operating under stringent energy, memory, and thermal constraints [9]. Classical real-time scheduling policies such as Earliest Deadline First (EDF) or Rate Monotonic (RM) are computationally lightweight but brittle under non-stationary workloads, bursty sensor streams, and varying wireless channel dynamics [1], [2]. Conversely, modern Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) approaches offer adaptivity but typically require computational resources (GPUs, large memory) unavailable on microcontroller-class hardware [3], [7], [8]. This paper bridges this gap by proposing a Hybrid Lightweight AI Scheduler (H-LAIS). H-LAIS combines a deterministic rule-based safety envelope, a highly quantized tiny neural inference core (distilled from a heavy teacher policy), and an ultra-compact RL adaptation layer to achieve ultra-fast, adaptive decision-making. The scheduler operates entirely on-device, consuming less than 15 kB of RAM and 30 kB of flash memory [4], [10]. The scheduling problem is formulated as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP) and solved using a Lagrangian relaxation technique that jointly accounts for deadline satisfaction, energy consumption, and context-aware urgency [13], [17]. Cycle-accurate simulations and hardware-in-the-loop experiments on an ARM Cortex-M4 platform demonstrate that H-LAIS reduces deadline misses by up to 41.3% and energy per decision by 32.7% compared to classical heuristics, while maintaining a worst-case inference latency under 40 µs. Furthermore, a Lyapunov stability analysis is provided to argue queue boundedness [17], and an extensive ablation study validates the system’s robustness.

Abstract: As deep learning, edge computing, and wearable sensing technologies have advanced, vision-based assistive navigation systems have evolved rapidly. This review focuses on the trade-offs between detection accuracy, latency, edge deployment feasibility, and human-centered evaluation by critically examining recent studies on vision-based navigation systems for blind and visually impaired individuals. We suggest a unified four-layer evaluation framework that incorporates algorithmic, system-level, user-level, and safety-level metrics in order to overcome this limitation. Lastly, we present a systematic research roadmap for improving assistive navigation systems by enhancing edge efficiency, reliability, and real-world validation. The goal of this review is to reorient the field toward deployable, user-centered, and safety-aware assistive technologies.

Abstract: This letter takes a first step towards the analysis of safety and performance critical computational tasks for autonomous robots. Our contribution is a safety-performance (SP) metric that ensures safety first and then rewards improved performance of real-time computational tasks, building on the notion of “nominal safety” which defines timely computation as critical to safety. To fully utilize the computing capacity of heterogeneous processing units (e.g., CPU + GPU), a computational task graph model called the Stochastic Heterogeneous Parallel Directed Acyclic Graph (SHP-DAG) is adopted to capture the uncertain nature of robotic applications and their required computation. Our SP metric is defined upon this task model, which allows us to apply the FIFO and CFS schedulers of the Linux kernel on complex robotic computational tasks and compare the SP metric with baseline metrics, average and worst-case makespan. Extensive experimental results on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Xavier hardware demonstrate that the proposed SP metric is appropriate for managing computational tasks in a manner that balances safety and performance in robotic systems.

Abstract: Multi-object tracking is a crucial task in computer vision, requiring real-time performance, accurate identification, and tracking multiple objects in a scene. However, it is a challenging process due to the large number of objects to track, the need to maintain their identities over time, and the complexity of deep neural networks. To address these challenges, we present an optimized multi-object tracking pipeline using TensorRT. We leverage ByteTrack, a state-of-the-art multi-object tracking framework, and implement the pipeline in C++ for low latency. We optimized the Yolox neural network used in ByteTrack with TensorRT to produce bounding boxes for each frame. We also focus on the fact that ByteTrack utilizes sparse matrices when applying a Kalman filter to generate tracklets for each object. We evaluate the performance of our approach on the palace.mp4 video dataset, which is used in the ByteTrack demo. Our experimental results show a significant improvement in frame rate, increasing from 10.1fps to 14.3fps, while also reducing memory consumption from 1.4GB to 1.1GB. Overall, our optimized multi-object tracking pipeline demonstrates the effectiveness of combining deep learning with TensorRT and classic computer vision techniques. It provides an efficient and accurate solution for real-world multi-object tracking applications, such as surveillance, robotics, and autonomous vehicles.

Authors: S. Han; K. Jun; D. -W. Lee

Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are effective at static image reasoning, but existing VLM-based safety systems remain biased toward static posture recognition (e.g., lying or sitting) rather than dynamic event understanding. In robotics, this distinction is critical because recognizing a state alone is insufficient to determine whether an event has actually occurred. Assistive robots require continuous monitoring and prompt responses to safety-critical transitions, which demands process-level reasoning. However, single-frame inference lacks temporal context, while video-based multi-frame pipelines are often computationally heavy for low-latency, on-device deployment. To address this gap, we propose SFC-VLM (Single-Frame Compression for Vision-Language Models), a framework that transforms temporal reasoning into spatial reasoning by compressing consecutive frames into a single image for event-level understanding. SFC-VLM employs two compression methods: Grid Compression (time represented as spatial order) and Motion Trail Compression (time represented through progressive fade/blur), along with compression-aware prompting that guides the model to leverage spatial reasoning for interpreting temporal sequences. We evaluate SFC-VLM on the Le2i Fall Detection Dataset using frame-level classification at 10 FPS. Grid Compression with a $2 \times 3$ grid layout achieves 58.06 F1 score, representing a 40% improvement over the no-compression baseline (41.49), while maintaining 97.00% specificity. Latency analysis shows that Grid Compression achieves an average event response time of 0.465 s and an average detection latency of 0.158 s, suggesting its potential as a low-latency temporal compression approach for robotic perception with only one VLM inference per decision.

Abstract: Asynchronous acoustic–visual tracking for uncrewed aerial systems (UAS) is constrained not only by sensor noise, but also by temporally inconsistent measurements caused by acoustic propagation delay, visual pipeline latency, jitter, dropout, and out-of-sequence packet arrivals. At the validated 200 Hz operating point, the proposed kernel achieves  $1.2~\pm ~0.2$  m RMSE with no injected delay,  $1.8~\pm ~0.3$  m RMSE at 100 ms delay, and  $3.9~\pm ~0.6$  m RMSE at 500 ms delay, while maintaining 0% lock loss and zero deadline misses. Abstract: Event-based vision has emerged as a promising paradigm for energy-aware artificial intelligence (AI), offering sparse, low-latency visual signals that reduce redundant data processing and support sustainable edge computing. However, the asynchronous and noise-prone nature of event streams creates challenges for conventional deep learning models, which are often too computationally intensive for low-power embedded platforms. This work presents a compact and configurable event-driven autoencoder (AE) that efficiently compresses neuromorphic data while preserving essential spatiotemporal structure for downstream inference. The architecture integrates lightweight convolutional encoding with robust performance under adaptive event thresholding and a minimal classifier head, enabling substantial reductions in computational cost without degrading recognition fidelity. Extensive evaluations on the smart event face dataset (SEFD) and event-based crossing dataset (EBCD) show that the proposed framework achieves competitive or superior accuracy compared to YOLOv9 while requiring up to  $35.6\times $  fewer parameters. To assess real-world sustainability, the model is deployed on resource-constrained hardware: a Raspberry Pi 4B and an NVIDIA Jetson Nano. On NVIDIA Jetson Nano, it delivers real-time throughput of 44.8 frames/s. On a Raspberry Pi 4B CPU, the 50% AE classifier consumes 16.19 J for the evaluated inference workload, corresponding to approximately  $726.3\times $  lower energy consumption than YOLOv9 under the same evaluation protocol. These results demonstrate the potential of compact event-driven models to advance environmentally conscious, low-power AI systems for high-speed perception in autonomous, mobile, and embedded computing environments.

Publication Title: 2026 IEEE 50th Annual Computers, Software, and Applications Conference (COMPSAC)
Abstract: Traffic congestion significantly impacts safety and urban livability in smart cities, motivating the development of accurate Traffic Flow Prediction (TFP) systems. Traditional deep learning approaches typically rely on centralized training, which is difficult to scale in distributed Internet of Things (IoT) environments. To address these limitations, decentralized paradigms such as Local Learning (LL) and Federated Learning (FL) enable on-device training and collaborative model updates while preserving data locality. For real-time TFP, the inherently non-stationary nature of traffic data necessitates continuous model adaptation, making online federated learning essential for scalable and collaborative deployment. However, this setting remains challenging because traffic data are typically non-IID across clients, with local patterns varying significantly across locations and devices. This paper presents an exploratory study of online federated learning for TFP on resource-constrained IoT devices. Using a GRU-based network as a common backbone, the Online Federated Learning paradigm is benchmarked relative to Centralized and Local Learning as reference baselines. A performance evaluation was conducted by evaluating RMSE and MAE on the PEMS-BAY dataset. Robustness to non-IID data is further assessed using FedProx and SCAFFOLD. Results show that LL achieves the lowest prediction error, whereas FL degrades as the number of local epochs increases, and non-IID mitigation strategies provide limited improvements under low-latency constraints. Overall, online federated learning is a viable approach for real-time TFP, but its performance is highly sensitive to client heterogeneity.

Abstract: This research presents the development and evaluation of an IoT-based nursing home monitoring system designed to enhance elderly healthcare through real-time detection, predictive alerts, and caregiver support. The system integrates multimodal sensing with edge and server-level machine learning to monitor three critical areas: sleep quality, fall detection, and emotion recognition in dementia patients. Hardware components, including a Raspberry Pi and non-intrusive sensors, were combined with lightweight neural networks to ensure low-latency processing. Detailed model optimizations, including 8-bit quantized TensorFlow Lite MobileNetV2 and CNN-LSTM pipelines, enabled on-device inference within 80–120 ms. A caregiver dashboard and mobile application provided intuitive visualization of real-time alerts and long-term health reports. Benchmarking against threshold-based and classical ML baselines demonstrated 9-18% performance improvements and 56% lower alert latency. Experimental evaluation demonstrated promising outcomes, with fall detection achieving 95% accuracy, emotion detection 91%, and sleep monitoring 90% reliability. System uptime reached 98%, and alerts were delivered within two seconds in 96% of cases. These results indicate that the proposed solution can effectively reduce caregiver burden, improve resident safety, and establish a scalable framework for intelligent elderly healthcare monitoring.

Abstract: The rapid growth of the aging population has intensified the need for intelligent systems that ensure safety, independence, and timely healthcare support for elderly individuals. This paper presents an integrated framework for activity recognition and assisted monitoring in elderly homes using Edge-AI. The proposed system combines real-time pose estimation, machine learning based activity classification, and IoT-enabled alert mechanisms deployed on a compact edge server. The edge server performs on-device inference using an optimized XGBoost classifier to distinguish normal daily activities from potential fall events. Skeletal key points are extracted using MediaPipe Pose and processed for robust activity recognition. Upon detecting a fall, the system triggers immediate alert notifications to remote caregivers for timely intervention. By operating entirely on edge infrastructure, the proposed system achieves low-latency response, enhanced data privacy, and reduced reliance on cloud connectivity. A lightweight dashboard interface further enables visualization of activity logs for long-term behavioral monitoring and trend analysis. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed Edge-AI framework offers a cost-effective, responsive, and scalable solution for intelligent elderly care in resourceconstrained environments.

Abstract: The rapid adoption of data-driven technologies is transforming modern agriculture, with Precision Livestock Farming (PLF) emerging as a key enabler of sustainable and efficient practices. While advances in computer vision, deep learning, and IoT have significantly improved animal identification, body condition scoring, and lameness detection, existing systems remain constrained by species-specific designs, reliance on cloud-based processing, and limited real-time responsiveness. This paper presents the Automated Cattle Detection and Risk Mitigation System, a novel three-tier edge-cloud architecture that integrates low-power edge devices with real-time cloud synchronization and intelligent alerting. At its core, the system utilizes a quantized YOLOv11 model on a Raspberry Pi 4B with TPU acceleration, achieving an inference rate of at least 18 FPS while consuming less than 5 W of power. The model is trained explicitly for multi-species detection, covering cattle, sheep, horses, humans, and predators, with an overall accuracy exceeding 94%. Field trials spanning 72 hours demonstrated robust accuracy, energy efficiency, and affordability, outperforming legacy RFID and cloud-dependent solutions. By bridging AI-driven monitoring with farmer-friendly interfaces, the proposed system enhances livestock safety, welfare, and operational resilience, offering a scalable framework for next-generation smart farming.

Abstract: AI visual aids and integrated reading assistants remain limited in accessibility and deployment for most blind people. Research on these topics is still fragmented across different data sets, tasks, and devices. Results for latency, energy, and longitudinal usability are also limited, with diverse measurement criteria. A complete end-to-end synthesis of the pipeline-capture, enhancement, layout analysis, recognition, semantics, and feedback, optimized for access, safety, and deployment -is systematically examined in this review. The study outlines open questions regarding multilingual scripts, curved or reflective text, and cluttered scenes. Functionalities are related to actual needs such as hands-free operation, offline service, ambiguity handling, and privacy protection. To enable fair comparison and reproducibility, evaluation practices are considered. Task-level metrics (time to first utterance, task success) and model-level metrics (precision-recall, character and word error rates) have been proposed. Clear guidelines for reporting datasets, protocols, error taxonomies, and user studies have also been provided. The review also links algorithmic efficiency techniques achieving low-latency, on-device operation to hardware constraints, e.g., NPUs, DSPs, thermal envelopes, and battery constraints. To understand the key issues and identify priority needs, this study presents shared definitions, minimum expectations, and practical checklists for researchers, clinicians, and developers by synthesising evidence across phones, wearables, and dedicated devices. The result is a framework and roadmap for sustainable and scalable reading support that describes what works, for whom, when, and why, with measurable benefits for real-world settings across countries.

Abstract: Wearable healthcare devices continuously capture diverse biosignals (ECG, PPG, EEG, EMG, and IMU data) that can enable early detection, continuous monitoring, and personalized intervention. Traditional signal-processing and deep-learning approaches treat biosignals as sequences or images, often neglecting the inherent relational and topological structure among sensors, anatomical sites, and temporal segments. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) provide a principled framework to encode such relational information, fuse multimodal streams, and perform inference with explicit modeling of inter-sensor and inter-feature dependencies. This paper presents a comprehensive treatment of GNN architectures, representation strategies, and optimization techniques tailored for real-time biosignal analysis in wearable systems. We (1) formalize biosignal-to-graph transformations that preserve physiological adjacency and functional coupling, (2) evaluate spatial, temporal, and spatio-temporal GNN variants for latency-constrained tasks (arrhythmia detection, cuffless blood-pressure estimation, EEG-based event detection, and activity recognition), (3) propose lightweight graph convolution and message-passing modules designed for edge inference and energy-efficient deployment, and (4) assess robustness to noise, missing channels, and variable sampling using both open benchmarks and a curated wearable dataset. Results demonstrate that appropriately constructed GNNs improve detection accuracy and calibration while reducing feature-engineering requirements, and that model pruning, quantization, and architecture search enable real-time inference on resource-limited wearable hardware. We conclude with a roadmap addressing clinical validation, privacy-preserving ondevice learning, and standardization of graph construction for reproducible biosignal GN

Abstract: This paper investigates AI-Native 6G networks that integrate deep reinforcement learning (DRL) agents at the network edge to achieve adaptive, low-latency, and energy-efficient resource allocation. We present a conceptual architecture—Edge-Integrated DRL (EIDRL)—that combines lightweight on-device policies, edge-hosted value models, and a hierarchical orchestration layer that mediates model updates, inference placement, and safety constraints. The proposed framework explicitly addresses 6G-era characteristics: massive heterogeneous devices, semantic and sensing-aided communications, integration of sensing/communication/computation (ISCC), and stringent reliability/latency requirements. We detail the learning formulation (state, action, reward, multi-timescale update rules), introduce techniques for sample-efficient training (model-based rollouts, transfer from foundation WLAMs, and federated/split learning hybrids), and propose mechanisms for safety, fairness, and compute-aware scheduling. Through analytical arguments and representative numerical scenarios (multi-tenant edge slices, ISAC nodes, and mobile user clusters), we demonstrate that EIDRL reduces regret relative to static baselines, lowers average latency under load, and improves spectral and energy efficiency when the edge controller coordinates inference placement and action aggregation. Finally, we identify open research directions—privacy-preserving multi-agent coordination, certifiable robustness of learned policies, semantics-aware reward design, and operational considerations for O-RAN/OAI integration—thereby providing a focused research agenda for adaptive resource allocation in AI-native 6G systems.
